summary.title: Dimeric cyclobutane formation under continuous flow conditions using organophotoredox catalysed [2+2]-cycloaddition
summary.authors: Helena F Grantham; Marc C Kimber; M F C Grantham; Kimber
summary.field_subfield: Organic Chemistry; Photoredox Catalysis; Continuous Flow Chemistry
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a merged methodology combining organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology to synthesize dimeric cyclobutanes, specifically focusing on carbazole derivatives and lignan natural products. The primary objective was to improve upon traditional batch conditions, which often require cryogenic temperatures, long reaction times, and higher catalyst loadings. The authors utilized a commercial continuous flow platform to perform [2+2]-cycloadditions of electron-rich alkenes, such as vinyl carbazole (VCZ) and E-asarone. A key finding is the significant reduction in catalyst loading, achieving a 79% isolated yield of 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB) using only 0.1 mol% of the organophotoredox catalyst, a substantial improvement over the 3 mol% typically required in batch reactions. The continuous flow process also drastically reduced reaction times, with optimal conditions achieving completion in under one hour compared to days in batch settings. The scope of the methodology was expanded to include functionalized vinyl carbazoles, such as brominated and arylated derivatives, which were successfully dimerized to create new classes of functional materials. Additionally, the protocol was applied to the synthesis of styrene-based lignan natural products, including magnosalin, without the need for cryogenic conditions or complex electron relays in some cases. The study demonstrates that continuous flow offers advantages in scalability, efficiency, and environmental sustainability, providing a robust route for the synthesis of valuable photophysical host materials and natural products. The work highlights the potential of merging sustainable catalytic methods with flow technology to overcome limitations of conventional batch chemistry.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a merged methodology combining organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology to synthesize dimeric cyclobutanes, specifically focusing on carbazole derivatives and lignan natural products. The primary objective was to improve upon traditional batch conditions, which often require cryogenic temperatures, long reaction times, and higher catalyst loadings. The authors utilized a commercial continuous flow platform to perform [2+2]-cycloadditions of electron-rich alkenes, such as vinyl carbazole (VCZ) and E-asarone. A key finding is the significant reduction in catalyst loading, achieving a 79% isolated yield of 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB) using only 0.1 mol% of the organophotoredox catalyst, a substantial improvement over the 3 mol% typically required in batch reactions. The continuous flow process also drastically reduced reaction times, with optimal conditions achieving completion in under one hour compared to days in batch settings. The scope of the methodology was expanded to include functionalized vinyl carbazoles, such as brominated and arylated derivatives, which were successfully dimerized to create new classes of functional materials. Additionally, the protocol was applied to the synthesis of styrene-based lignan natural products, including magnosalin, without the need for cryogenic conditions or complex electron relays in some cases. The study demonstrates that continuous flow offers advantages in scalability, efficiency, and environmental sustainability, providing a robust route for the synthesis of valuable photophysical host materials and natural products. The work highlights the potential of merging sustainable catalytic methods with flow technology to overcome limitations of conventional batch chemistry.

Research Context
Dimerization of electron-rich alkenes provides a route to cyclobutanes. Vinyl carbazole is a precursor for t-DCzCB host materials. Traditional methods include chemical oxidation or photochemical dimerization. Organophotoredox catalysis offers sustainability advantages over metal catalysts. Previous organophotoredox methods required cryogenic conditions and high loadings. Continuous flow technology improves irradiation efficiency in photoredox reactions. Prior work used heterogeneous photoredox fixed bed flow processes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to merge organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow. It is hypothesized that flow will improve yield and reduce time. The goal is to synthesize t-DCzCB and functional analogues. The authors anticipate a convenient and environmentally beneficial methodology. The study seeks to showcase advantages over batch chemistry. It is predicted that catalyst loadings can be significantly reduced. The methodology is expected to apply to lignan natural products.

Methodological Details
The study used a commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform. Batch synthesis used 3 mol% catalyst and cryogenic temperatures. Optimization was performed using HPLC analysis with p-terphenyl standard. Optimal flow rate was 0.5 mL.min-1 with 20 min residence time. Irradiation was performed at 450 nm, 405 nm, and 420 nm. The reaction was scaled to 10 mmol of vinyl carbazole. Catalyst loading was reduced to 0.1 mol% for the scale-up. Vinyl carbazoles were synthesized using the method of Obora. Concentration was reduced to 0.2 M for substituted substrates. Electron relays like anthracene were used for styrene dimerization.

Procedures And Architectures
The flow system used a residence time of 20 minutes. The reaction mixture was 0.4 M in acetone for VCZ. The catalyst was a pyrillium organophotoredox compound. Flow rates were varied to probe reaction reversibility. The system was deoxygenated for batch reactions. HPLC calibration was performed for quantification. The flow apparatus was a commercial platform. Irradiation wavelengths were tested for catalyst absorbance. Styrene dimerization required an electron relay. The flow rate for substituted carbazoles was 0.2 mL.min-1.

Key Results
Batch synthesis of t-DCzCB yielded 82% isolated product. Optimal flow conditions gave 98% yield at 2 mol% catalyst. Reducing catalyst to 1 mol% gave 93% yield. Lowering flow rate to 2 mL.min-1 reduced yield to 79%. Very low flow rate of 0.1 mL.min-1 gave 53% yield. Scale-up at 0.1 mol% catalyst gave 79% isolated yield. 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole dimerized to 64% yield in flow. Batch dimerization of 3-bromo substrate gave 48% yield. 4-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole dimerized to improved yields in flow. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole did not dimerize. 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole dimerized to 65% yield in flow. 2-chloro-9-vinylcarbazole dimerized to 61% yield. 2-methoxy-9-vinylcarbazole dimerized to 45% yield. Bis-vinylated 2-hydroxycarbazole dimerized to 25% yield. 2-arylated vinylcarbazole 22a dimerized to 65% yield. Tetra-alkyl substituted dimer 23b was obtained in 57% yield. 3,6-bisarylated dimer 24b was obtained in 50% yield. Suzuki coupling of 13b gave 75% yield of 25. Borylation of 13b gave 36% yield of 26. 4-methoxy styrene dimerized to 44% yield. Styrene 29 dimerized to 22% yield of pellucidin A. E-asarone dimerized to 40% yield of magnosalin.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Continuous flow allows for more efficient irradiation. Reduced catalyst loading indicates higher catalytic efficiency. The method provides a route to novel functional materials. The protocol is scalable and environmentally beneficial. Flow conditions avoid the need for cryogenic temperatures. The method showcases advantages over conventional batch chemistry. The approach is robust and general for cyclobutane synthesis.

Contradictions And Limitations
Solubility of substituted vinyl carbazoles in acetone was challenging. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole failed to dimerize. Longer residence times led to background oxidation. Some yields were modest, such as 25% for bis-enolether. The mechanism of reversibility was inferred, not directly proven.

Claims
Continuous flow organophotoredox catalysis improves yield and reduces catalyst loading compared to batch. Flow gave 98% yield vs 82% in batch. Catalyst loading reduced to 0.1 mol%. Reaction times were significantly reduced. Some substituted substrates had lower yields in flow. The method is more sustainable and efficient.
The methodology is applicable to a wide scope of functionalized carbazoles and styrenes. Brominated, chlorinated, and arylated substrates were dimerized. Lignan natural products were synthesized. 1-bromo substrate failed to dimerize. New functional materials can be accessed.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Flow rate variations were tested to probe reversibility. Different wavelengths (405, 420, 450 nm) were tested. Absence of catalyst or light stopped the reaction. Electron relays improved styrene dimerization outcomes.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 details the optimization study of flow conditions. Scheme 1 shows cyclobutane dimers as functional materials. Scheme 2 illustrates the radical cation mechanism. Scheme 3 shows the merged flow and organophotoredox protocol. Scheme 4 shows the batch vs flow comparison for VCZ. Scheme 5 shows the substrate scope for carbazoles. Scheme 6 shows the synthetic potential of bromocyclobutanes. Scheme 7 shows the dimerization of styrenes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a merged flow/organophotoredox protocol. 2. The strongest evidence is the 0.1 mol% catalyst loading. 3. The future path is synthesis of new functional materials.
